# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XV. MORE GOSSIP

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Miss Winifred and Mary Stubbs journeyed to Hollowmere on the evening following the burial of Mrs. Myra Murray from the over-harbour section. Miss Winifred desired to relieve her spirit regarding various matters. Naturally, the complete details of the funeral required thorough discussion. Miss Winifred and Tabitha debated this topic back and forth; Nell found no pleasure in these gruesome dialogues and refrained from joining in. Sitting slightly separated from them, she observed the dahlias' fall glow throughout the garden, alongside the serene, enchanting harbor framed by the September sunset. Mary Stubbs was seated next to her, quietly engaged in knitting. Although Mary's thoughts were anchored down in the Fern Hollow, where gentle, muted echoes of laughing children drifted from, Miss Winifred kept watch over her hands. A set quantity of stocking rounds had to be completed prior to her departure for the valley. Mary continued her knitting and remained silent, though she listened attentively.
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0000 }

“No deceased person ever possessed a finer appearance,” stated Miss Winifred with expert judgment. “A lovely female was what Myra Murray had constantly been—her maiden name was Corey from Kettlebridge, a family famed for being handsome.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0001 }

“When I went by the body, I uttered to it, ‘poor woman. I wish you to be as joyous as you appear.’” Tabitha exhaled. “She was not greatly altered. The gown on her was the black satin acquired fourteen years back for the marriage of her daughter. At that time, her Aunt advised her to save it for her burial, yet Myra chuckled and replied, ‘I might be dressed in it for my burial, Aunty, but I shall enjoy myself in it beforehand.’ And it is fair to state she accomplished that. Myra Murray was not the type of person to go to her own burial prior to her death. On numerous occasions later on, observing her having a fine time among others, I reflected to myself, ‘You are a fine-looking woman, Myra Murray, and that gown suits you, yet it will probably end up as your burial clothes.’ And as you can observe, my statement has proven accurate, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0002 }

Tabitha let out another deep sigh. She was having a wonderful time. Discussing a funeral was truly an enjoyable topic.
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0003 }

“I was always fond of seeing Myra,” Miss Winifred stated. “She possessed such constant gaiety and cheerfulness—her greeting alone sufficed to improve your spirits. Myra invariably turned everything to good account.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0004 }

“That is correct,” Tabitha affirmed. “I was informed by her sister-in-law that upon being finally notified by the physician that his efforts were futile and her confinement to that bed was permanent, Myra remarked with considerable cheer, ‘Well, if such is the case, I am grateful that all the preserving has been completed, and I am spared from undergoing the autumn house-cleaning. Spring house-cleaning was always to my liking,’ she remarks, ‘whereas I invariably despised doing it in the autumn. Thank goodness, I shall escape it this year.’ Certain individuals might label such a remark as lightmindedness, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr, and it seemed to me that her sister-in-law felt somewhat embarrassed by it. She suggested that Myra’s illness might have rendered her somewhat delirious. However, I replied, ‘No, Mrs. Murray, let this not distress you. It was merely Myra’s manner of seeing the positive side.’”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0005 }

“Her sister Luella was the exact reverse,” Miss Winifred said. “Luella saw no bright side—for her, only black and gray shades existed. Throughout many years, she was constantly asserting that her death would occur within about a week. ‘I won’t be here to burden you long,’ she was accustomed to telling her family while groaning. Furthermore, if a single one of them dared to speak of their modest upcoming plans, she would groan as well and utter, ‘Ah, I won’t be here then.’ Whenever I visited her, I invariably concurred with her statements, which infuriated her to the point that she became considerably improved for a number of days following. Her health is superior now, yet she possesses no additional cheerfulness. Myra differed greatly. Making somebody feel good through her actions or words was her constant habit. It may be that the husbands they wedded were partially responsible. Luella’s husband was a Tartar, take my word for it, whereas Saul Murray was respectable, as far as men are concerned. He appeared grief-stricken today. Feeling pity for a man during the burial of his wife is a rare thing for me, yet my sympathies truly went out to Saul Murray.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0006 }

“It is no surprise that he appeared mournful. A spouse such as Myra will not come his way again anytime soon,” Tabitha remarked. “Perhaps he will refrain from trying, given that his offspring are fully grown and Mirabel can manage the home. However, one cannot foresee the actions of a widower, and I, personally, shall not attempt to.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0007 }

“Myra will be terribly missed by us in church,” Miss Winifred remarked. “She was a true worker. She was never stumped by anything. Whenever a difficulty couldn’t be gotten over by her, she’d get around it, and whenever she couldn’t get around it, she’d act like it didn’t exist—and usually it didn’t. ‘I’ll keep a stiff upper lip to my journey’s end,’ she stated to me one time. Well, her journey has been ended by her.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0008 }

“Is that what you believe?” inquired Nell abruptly, returning from her daydream. “I am unable to imagine her travels having come to a close. Are you able to envision her seated with her hands folded—that earnest, inquiring soul she possessed, along with its splendid, daring perspective? No, it is my belief that when she died she simply unlocked a portal and passed across—forward—forward—toward fresh, brilliant quests.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0009 }

“Maybe—maybe,” Miss Winifred agreed. “Do you know, Nell dearie, I myself was never very drawn to this eternal rest doctrine—although I hope saying so isn’t heresy. In heaven, I want to bustle around just like here. And I hope pies and doughnuts will have a celestial equivalent—something that requires BEING MADE. Naturally, a person does grow terribly tired at times—and you grow tireder the older you get. But you would think the very tiredest could become rested in less time than eternity—except, perhaps, for a lazy man.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0010 }

“I want to see Myra Murray, when I encounter her once more,” Nell said, “approaching me in her usual brisk and laughing manner, exactly as she continually used to do in this place.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0011 }

“Oh, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha remarked, sounding horrified, “you certainly cannot believe that Myra is going to be laughing in the next life?”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0012 }

“What is the reason, Tabitha? Is it your belief that our tears will fall in that place?”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0013 }

“No, no, Mrs. Dr. dear, do not misinterpret my meaning. It is my belief that we will neither be weeping nor laughing.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0014 }

“Then what?”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0015 }

“Well,” said Tabitha, forced into speaking, “Mrs. Dr. dear, I believe that our only course is to appear devout and grave.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0016 }

“And do you truly believe, Tabitha,” inquired Nell, appearing sufficiently grave, “that either Myra Murray or myself could appear grave and pious constantly—constantly, Tabitha?”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0017 }

“Well,” Tabitha conceded hesitantly, “I could perhaps agree that each of you would need to grin occasionally, yet I am unable to ever acknowledge that laughter exists in heaven. That notion appears truly disrespectful, Mrs. Dr. dear.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0018 }

“Well, returning to earth,” Miss Winifred said, “who is available for us to secure for Myra’s class in Sunday School? Since Myra fell ill, Julia Clow has been its teacher, but with her moving to town for the winter, we must acquire someone else.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0019 }

“I was told that Mrs. Laurie Jamieson was interested in it,” Nell remarked. “Since relocating to the Glen from Kettlebridge, the Jamiesons have attended church on a very regular basis.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0020 }

“Fresh sweepers!” expressed Miss Winifred with hesitation. “Hold off until they have attended consistently over twelve months.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0021 }

“Mrs. Dr. dear, Mrs. Jamieson is not someone you can rely on at all,” Tabitha remarked with gravity. “Having passed away on one occasion, she actually returned to life right when they were taking her measurements for a coffin, following a truly lovely laying out! So, Mrs. Dr. dear, it is clear that a woman of that sort is not to be depended upon.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0022 }

“It’s possible she could become a Methodist whenever,” Miss Winifred remarked. “I am informed that they attended the Methodist Church in Kettlebridge just as frequently as the Presbyterian one. So far, I haven't seen them doing so in this place, but allowing Mrs. Jamieson to join the Sunday School would not meet with my approval. Even so, causing them offense is something we cannot do. Too many of our members are being lost, either because they die or lose their tempers. Having departed from the church, Mrs. Hector Twiss left without anybody understanding the reason. The managers were informed by her that Mr. Ashdown’s salary would never receive another cent from her. Naturally, the majority of folks claim she was insulted by the children, yet I somehow doubt that. Although I attempted to elicit information from Grace, the only thing she revealed was that Mrs. Twiss arrived to visit her father, appearing in very pleasant spirits, and departed in a terrible fury, referring to every one of them as ‘varmints!’”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0023 }

“Varmints, indeed!” Tabitha exclaimed in an angry manner. “Is Mrs. Hector Twiss forgetting that the uncle she had through her mother was believed to have poisoned his spouse? It was never actually proven, my dear Mrs. Dr., and one shouldn't trust everything one hears. Nevertheless, were I to possess an uncle whose spouse passed away with no clear cause, I wouldn't travel across the land referring to blameless youths as varmints.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0024 }

“It comes down to this,” Miss Winifred stated, “that a substantial subscription was provided by Mrs. Twiss, and covering that deficit presents a real difficulty. Furthermore, should she manage to influence the remaining Fairlies against Mr. Ashdown, which she undoubtedly will attempt, his departure will be inevitable.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0025 }

“I do not believe Mrs. Hector Twiss is particularly popular among the other members of the family,” Tabitha remarked. “She probably will not manage to affect their thinking.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0026 }

“However, those Fairlies are all so united. Should you affect one, you affect them all. It is beyond doubt that we cannot manage without them. One half of the salary comes from them. Whatever other accusations are made against them, they are not stingy. Before his departure long ago, Lionel Fairlie was accustomed to contribute a hundred every year.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0027 }

“Why did he depart?” inquired Nell.
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0028 }

“He stated that a deal involving a cow was cheated out of him by a member of the session. For twenty years, he has failed to attend church. While she was living, poor thing, his wife brought herself regularly, yet he insisted she never contribute anything beyond a single red cent each Sunday. She experienced terrible humiliation. I am not certain if his treatment of her as a husband was particularly good, even if no complaints were ever heard from her. However, her expression was invariably cowed. Thirty years ago, the woman desired by Lionel Fairlie was not the one he obtained, and second best was something the Fairlies never cared to tolerate.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0029 }

“Which woman was the one he actually desired.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0030 }

“Harriet Ainslie. Although they were not precisely engaged, if I am not mistaken, their companionship lasted for two years. Then their relationship abruptly ended—without anyone ever learning the reason. It was merely a foolish disagreement, in my opinion. Lionel then proceeded to marry Dinah Coyle prior to his anger subsiding—doing so solely to inflict hurt on Harriet, I am entirely convinced. Typical male behavior! While Dinah was a pleasant young woman, she lacked a strong will, and he crushed the slight resolve she possessed. Her docility was excessive for Lionel. A wife capable of confronting him was what he required. Harriet would have managed him splendidly, an arrangement he would have appreciated far more. The reality is that he held Dinah in contempt simply owing to her constant submission. Years ago, in his youth, I frequently overheard his declaration ‘Give me a spunky woman—spunk for me every time.’ Yet he subsequently chose a bride who lacked the courage to utter a word—just like a man. Every member of that Coyle family was a mere vegetable. Despite performing the routines of existence, they possessed no real vitality.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0031 }

“When Russell Coyle wed his second bride, he utilized the wedding-ring from his first,” Tabitha recalled. “In my judgment, Mrs. Dr. dear, that was overly frugal. Furthermore, John, who is his brother, erected his own gravestone in the graveyard over the harbour, complete with all details except his date of death, and he visits and gazes upon it each Sunday. While the majority of people would fail to see the pleasure in that, he clearly finds it enjoyable. Individuals certainly possess varied notions regarding what is fun. Turning to Lionel Fairlie, that man is a complete pagan. Upon being questioned by the previous minister about his complete absence from church, he answered ‘The women there are too unattractive, parson—far too unattractive!’ Mrs. Dr. dear, I would love to approach a person like that and gravely declare, ‘Hell truly exists!’”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0032 }

“Oh, Lionel denies the existence of such a location,” stated Miss Winifred. “It is my hope that his error becomes clear to him as he approaches death. Now, Mary, having completed your three knitted inches, you are permitted to join the children at play for thirty minutes.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0033 }

No further encouragement was required for Mary. With her heart matching the swiftness of her feet, she hurried to Fern Hollow, where, during their talk, she imparted every detail regarding Mrs. Hector Twiss to Grace Ashdown.
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0034 }

“And Mrs. Kerr states that she will cause every Fairlie to oppose your father, forcing him to depart from the Glen due to his salary going unpaid,” Mary ended. “Honest to goodness, I am at a loss as to what should be done. Things would not be quite so terrible if old Lionel Fairlie would simply return to church and resume paying. However, he will refuse to do so—the Fairlies will depart—and every one of you will be compelled to leave.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0035 }

Grace retired for the night with a burden of sorrow weighing upon her. It was impossible to endure the idea of departing from the Glen. The Carrows were companions unmatched anywhere on earth. Her young heart had experienced deep agony during their departure from Juneford—numerous painful tears had been wept by her as she said goodbye to her friends in Juneford and the ancient manse situated there, where her mother had spent her life and passed away. The prospect of experiencing a similar and even more painful separation was something she could not peacefully consider. Departing from Glen St. Agnes, beloved Fern Hollow, and that delightful cemetery was simply beyond her.
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0036 }

“Being a minister’s family is terrible,” Grace lamented, her face buried in her pillow. “The moment you begin to love a location, you get uprooted. I will never, ever, ever wed a minister, regardless of how wonderful he might be.”
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0037 }

Upright in her bed, Grace gazed through the small, vine-draped window. Nothing disturbed the profound stillness of the night except the gentle sound of Ida’s breath, leaving Grace with a dreadful sense of loneliness. Below her lay Glen St. Agnes, resting beneath the star-filled, azure expanses of the autumn sky. Across the valley, a lamp glowed in the girls’ bedroom at Hollowmere, while a second light beamed from the chamber belonging to Edmund, prompting Grace to wonder whether toothache was plaguing poor Edmund once more. A brief, envious sigh escaped her as she thought of Bess and Izzy, who possessed both a mother and an established home, unlike herself, exposed to the whims of individuals who flew into unprovoked rages and branded one a varmint. Farther past the Glen, surrounded by sleeping, silent pastures, yet another lamp flickered, which Grace recognized as emanating from the residence of Lionel Fairlie. According to rumor, he remained awake reading until the late hours of the night. Mary had remarked that if he could merely be persuaded to rejoin the church, harmony would be restored. What reason was there to doubt it? As Grace observed a prominent, low-lying star hovering above the high, sharp-topped spruce standing by the entrance of the Methodist Church, a sudden idea struck her. Understanding the necessary course of action, Grace Ashdown resolved that she herself would undertake it to rectify the entire situation. Contentedly sighing, she shifted away from the desolate, pitch-black world outside and snuggled up beside Ida.
{: #nw-v05-c15-p0038 }
